newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. challenges some new diplomatic parking rules.
newsitem.headline: U.N. challenges some new diplomatic parking rules.

text.p: Parts of a city plan requiring diplomats in New York to pay parking fines are inconsistent with international law but elements of the scheme should be welcomed, the U.N. legal counsel said on Wednesday.

Under a programme unveiled this month by Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and due to go into effect on April 1, diplomats failing to clear up their parking tickets within a year would lose their license plates until they paid up. Until now, no action has been taken against diplomats who ignored parking tickets although some paid fines voluntarily.

Under international law, diplomats are usually immune from prosecution and some U.N. missions have accumulated thousands of unpaid tickets, raising the ire of city officials and the resentment of many New Yorkers.

The U.N. legal counsel, in an eight-page opinion, said: "Generally the elements of the city programme are clearly within the scope of the host country's power to establish the laws and regulations governing the operation and parking of diplomatic vehicles and related matters and do not seem to raise objections under international law."
Parts of the programme "should even be welcomed as likely to reduce the current difficulty of diplomatic missions in securing parking and in voiding unjustified tickets," he said.

This was a reference to assurances that each mission would have two parking spaces and each ambassador's residence one space and that a new police "hot line" would be set up to report unauthorised vehicles using those parking spots. Diplomats would also be allowed to challenge improperly issued parking tickets with the city finance department.

The legal counsel took issue with plans to remove the license plates of vehicles towed away and non-release of those vehicles until certain conditions had been met such as payment of a fine and/or towing charge.

"In general, measures aimed at depriving a diplomatic agent of the right to drive by withdrawal of license plates, registration or other pertinent legal documents ... are tantamount to an exercise of jurisdiction of the host country and thus are in contravention" of some accords, he said.

He cited a 1961 Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations, a 1946 convention on the privileges and immunities of the United Nations, and a 1947 agreement between the United Nations and the United States governing the locating of U.N. headquarters in New York.

"More importantly, they would be inconsistent with the host country's obligation to facilitate the functioning of the missions accredited to the United Nations and of their members," the legal opinion said.
The opinion will be considered by the U.N. committee on relations with the host country, which deals with problems affecting U.N. missions and diplomats.
